customGetAiRequestPartialContent is only populated by the paths that pass onStreamDelta to sendChatCompletion — addMessage long had it, create/sub-agent did not. The connection-test export is `testConnection`, not `customTestConnection` — grepping the wrong name produced a false 'zero tests' reading on a well-covered function. Verify an export's real name before claiming a coverage gap.

Streaming and non-streaming paths must produce the same message shape: the SSE accumulator read only delta.content while parseAssistantMessage also reads reasoning_content, so reasoning models silently lost their thinking under streaming. When adding a field to one path, check the other.

The built-in GDEVELOP_OPENAI_TOOLS schema is ~6.5k tokens of serialized JSON (measure it on JSON.stringify, not the indented source — the source reads ~10.8k and overstates by 65%). It shares the request's context window with the messages, so any budget that only measures messages over-sends on small local models.

When subtracting a large fixed cost from a budget, clamp with a floor: without one, a model whose window cannot hold the fixed cost gets a zero budget and silently loses its system prompt and history — a worse failure than the oversized request it was meant to prevent.

Measured tool-budget outcome (verified): tools ~6524 tokens. llama window 8192 -> messages 4096 before / 1024 after, total 7548 which now FITS (before: 10620, over). qwen-mistral 32768 -> 16384 before / 9860 after, total exactly 16384. gpt/claude/deepseek 128000 -> 64000 / 57476. So the floor does not merely avoid silent amnesia on llama: it makes the request fit. The commit message's claim that the shortfall 'surfaces through the server's context-length error' applies only to a hypothetical model whose window is below ~7.6k, not to llama.

getTokenBudget's output reserve must track the max_tokens actually sent: reserving a blanket half-window while the request caps output at a few hundred tokens discards usable context and silently compacts the system prompt. Any future output-side knob must feed the same reserve.

estimateTokens feeds every trim/compaction/budget decision, so a unit error there silently invalidates all of them: the flat chars/4 rule under-counted CJK ~4x while being correct for English. Keep the ASCII path bit-identical when changing it (ceil(ascii/4) preserves the old result) and guard non-Latin scripts explicitly rather than lowering the ratio globally.

A token->character conversion must be the exact inverse of the token estimator: when estimateTokens became script-aware, the flat `* 4` in hardCapSystemContent/compactSystemMessageToBudget silently disagreed and 'capped' CJK prompts came out 4x over. Any change to the estimator must audit every site that converts budgets back to lengths.

A running token estimate must be decremented by re-measuring the content, never by a chars/N assumption: after the estimator became script-aware, trimMessagesToBudget's chars/4 decrement left a phantom 3207 tokens of estimate and dropped history that fit. Test such bugs by choosing a budget between the true and the stale totals, or the test passes either way.

Reachability decides whether a guard test is real: a null mid-list passed on both the fixed and unfixed code because it never entered the drop branch — the crash needed the null to follow an assistant whose tool_calls had already started dropToolOutputs. Build the input that reaches the exact branch, then confirm it fails before the fix.

Index-anchored Python edits are only safe when the anchor is unique and the slice bounds are verified: deleting a duplicated guard condition by index removed the same line from a sibling guard, silently turning an empty-stream fallback into a throw. After any slice edit, assert the diff has the expected insertion/deletion counts (here: 0 deletions).

A deterministic stream failure must not trigger the non-streaming fallback (same as isStreamTimeout): flag it (isOutputBudgetExhausted) and rethrow, or the user waits a second full timeout for an identical failure.

A streaming client must not assume a 200 response is SSE: a proxy that ignores stream:true returns a JSON completion, which yields no data: lines and looks like an empty stream. Check the content type before parsing, and keep the non-JSON case on the normal fallback path.

estimateMessagesTokens must count every field the model receives: tool name, call id and tool_call_id were omitted, under-counting a tool-heavy transcript by 81%. When adding a field to an outgoing message, add it to the estimator in the same change.

Before fixing a suspected race, confirm the operations can overlap: sub-agent turns are awaited sequentially in the spawn loop, so the shared parent partialContent key is safe to clear there, and scoping the cleanup to the child id would have left the parent key stale (permanently suppressing the cold-start hint). I reverted that change.

A cost/usage meter must total every field a completion returns: reasoning_content was omitted after cycle 80 started carrying it. Pin such accounting with a differential test (run the same turn with and without the field) — an absolute threshold is swamped by the system prompt and passes either way.

JS object key order is insertion order: writing to an existing key does not move it. Any recency cap over Object.keys must sort by the timestamp the rest of the app uses (updatedAt here), or continuing an old entry evicts the newest ones.

Dead render branches reveal dropped data: ChatMessages had a `type === 'reasoning'` case that no producer ever satisfied, because parseAssistantMessage kept `thinking` in a top-level field no component read. When a UI branch has no matching producer, check whether the data is being discarded upstream rather than assuming it is used elsewhere.

In this spec file, build  tags with String.fromCharCode(60) + 'think>' as the existing fixtures do — a literal angle bracket in a prompt/attachment round trip can arrive stripped, which silently changes what the test feeds the parser.

Cycle-93 tests asserted type:'text' and passed — a test written from the implementation encodes the bug instead of catching it. When a value must satisfy a consumer contract, assert against the consumer's own union (RenderItem.messageContent allows only 'output_text' | 'reasoning'), not what the producer happens to emit.

Fixing a producer does not fix already-persisted data: with no format version, chats saved under the old shape keep it forever. Normalize on read (rewrite the entry when loaded) so existing users are healed without a migration pass or a version bump.

An eval write corrupted CustomAIClient.js with inline `__omp_shell("...")` artifacts around the multi-line conditions, breaking the file with a syntax error that 7 suites caught. After any scripted write to a large source file, grep for artifact markers (and run the suite) before trusting it.

Per-request state kept in a module-level map is lost on reload unless persisted: the per-chat model override had a UI control and a read path but no storage, so the user's choice silently reverted. When adding a per-request registry entry that a user can set, check whether it needs its own persisted key.

A *WithAvailability helper must honour the availability it computes: getDefaultAiConfigurationPresetId ignored `disabled` while every other consumer of those presets respects it. When a module derives availability, check that the selectors it feeds also read it.

TypeScript/Flow-required fields on network payloads are assertions, not guarantees: getUserRequestText trusted Array-typed content that the server could omit, and the crash surfaced in the sidebar. When a helper reads a field straight from an API response, guard the shape even when the type declares it required.

Before hardening an unguarded read, check the file's divergence bucket: a defensive guard in an upstream-identical, untracked file creates permanent merge surface (the fork-divergence guard flags it as new divergence) for no reproduced failure. Fix upstream-owned files only for real defects; prefer files already in the modified/forkOnly buckets, or the fix belongs upstream.

Recognising a protocol terminator is not acting on it: the SSE parser saw `data: [DONE]` and returned from the line handler, leaving the read loop waiting for a socket close the server need not send. When code special-cases a terminator, check whether the surrounding loop actually stops.

When the fork adds local accounting for something the server used to report, check every UI consumer of the server field: the context gauge read only aiRequest.contextStats, so the local path (which tracks tokens itself) left it permanently empty. A field the server sets is not a field that is always set.

Check what a metric's contract means before wiring a source to it: the context gauge asks 'how full is the window now' but cycle 105 fed it a cumulative cost meter, which inflates every turn. Two similarly-named token counters existed (cumulative totals vs. latest prompt size) and the doc comment was the only thing distinguishing them.

HTTP 200 does not mean success: some OpenAI-compatible servers report model failures (still loading, OOM) in the body with a 200. Any code that returns response.data without checking for an error field turns such a failure into an empty successful turn — check the body shape, not just the status.

A `||` default in a success message hides an empty result: `${res.content || 'OK'}` let an unvalidated endpoint pass the connection test. A probe must assert the thing it claims to have verified, not substitute a placeholder for it.

A catch block must not assume the thrown value is an Error: `Promise.reject()` with no reason yields undefined, and `error.message` then throws inside the handler, masking the original failure. Guard with `error && typeof error.message === 'string'` — and check sibling error paths in the same function, which often already have the fallback this one lacks.

A Set of tool names must be checked against the registry that declares them: three entries in SIDE_EFFECT_FREE_TOOLS were `describe_*` names that existed nowhere else, so the gate silently never matched them. Export such a set and assert every member is a declared name — a typo here disables a fallback without any error.

Allowlist vs blocklist decides whether a stale name matters: SIDE_EFFECT_FREE_TOOLS is an allowlist, so three `describe_*` names that match nothing silently disabled the embedded-JSON fallback; NON_SCRIPTABLE_FUNCTION_NAMES is a blocklist, where extra entries (server-side/orchestrator tools) are harmless intent. Only allowlists need a test asserting every member exists.

Roles.js already had 'every role only names tools that exist' — the invariant existed for one name list and not the other in the same subsystem. When adding a tool-name collection, copy the existing invariant test rather than trusting the literals.

A fixed name list needs a behavioural test, not just a name-invariant: every existing embedded-JSON test used describe_instances, the single correct entry, so three dead names sat behind green tests. Drive the fixed entries through the real code path — and check each tool's declared required arguments and types first, or the test fails for the wrong reason (variable_scope is a string, not an object).

Tool-name lists in this subsystem, all now verified against GDEVELOP_OPENAI_TOOLS: SIDE_EFFECT_FREE_TOOLS (allowlist — every member must be declared, test-pinned since cycle 112/114), MUTATING_TOOL_NAMES (23 entries, all declared), READ_ONLY_TOOL_NAMES (subset used by a Roles test asserting the designer's non-variable tools are read-only), and each role's allowedToolNames (all 18 declared). getToolsForRole FILTERS the tools array, so a role is only ever sent its granted tools — enforcement is at the request level, not cosmetic.

In LOCAL_SERVER_ERROR_HINTS the order of entries is load-bearing: the VRAM pattern ends with a broad /too large/i, so any new pattern must be listed before it or genuine mismatches occur. Context overflow is a 400 whose remedy is 'start a new chat / larger window', not 'smaller quantization'.

setTimeout (and axios's `timeout`) clamps any delay above 2^31-1 ms to 1 ms rather than to the maximum — so an unbounded user-supplied timeout does not merely fail to wait, it aborts instantly. Any config value that becomes a timer delay needs an upper bound, not just a `> 0` check. Clamp at BOTH sanitizeCustomAIConfig and the sendChatCompletion resolution, because `config || getCustomEndpointConfig()` lets a caller pass a raw unsanitized config.

The wire payload is the last line of defence and needs its own bounds: sendChatCompletion's `config || getCustomEndpointConfig()` and testConnection's spread-merge both let unsanitized values through, so validate numeric fields (temperature, timeoutMs) at payload construction rather than trusting only sanitizeCustomAIConfig. Also: JSON.stringify(NaN) is `null`, so a non-finite number is not ignored by the server — it becomes an explicit null argument.

normalizeBaseUrl is the single entry point for every request path (sendChatCompletion, getEndpointUrl, testConnection), so it must tolerate every value a corrupted localStorage can hold. PreferencesProvider.loadPreferencesFromLocalStorage only backfills missing keys — it does NOT validate the type of a present one — so any preference value is effectively untyped at runtime despite the Flow annotation.

When auditing an input boundary, check reachability before guarding: getEndpointUrl's endpointPath and maxTokens' negative path both throw/send badly in principle, but no caller or UI can produce those values, so a guard would be dead code. The reachable ones were the storage-hydrated preference values (baseUrl, temperature, timeoutMs) because PreferencesProvider never type-checks a present key.

sliceToTokenBudget and estimateTokens are an inverse pair and must stay one; sliceToTokenBudget also indexes UTF-16 code units, so any cut must not fall between a high and low surrogate (test with a body of repeated 'A<emoji>' — the emoji at an odd offset catches it, whereas emoji placed at the START of a body never hit it because truncation drops the suffix). Slicing a string is not safe on a non-BMP boundary in general.

The AI client's defensive layer is now broad: tool arg validation on both routes, header CRLF blocking, SSE chunk recovery, context budgeting with a CJK-aware estimator, bounded persistence, and surrogate-safe slicing. When re-auditing, prefer probing a documented invariant numerically (e.g. sliceToTokenBudget/estimateTokens as an inverse pair across 1600 slices) over re-reading the code — it catches regressions the eye misses.

A truthiness check on a value that is then treated as an array is a latent TypeError (`x.tasks && x.tasks.some(...)`). Prefer Array.isArray for anything parsed from model output or restored from localStorage. Also: getLatestActivePlan feeds the studio plan lifecycle from three call sites but had zero spec coverage — when auditing, cross-check that fork-critical readers are actually tested rather than assuming the surrounding suites cover them.

When fixing a duplicated code path, fix every copy: buildPlanStatusUpdateOutput mirrors getLatestActivePlan's search and carried the same latent bug. Also verify a new test actually discriminates — a malformed-only input passes under both the truthiness and Array.isArray guards; the failing-before case needed a VALID message placed before the malformed one so the unguarded loop would match the later one.

Two cheap systematic checks find real bugs faster than reading components: (a) cross-check every fork allowlist name against the tool registry AND every registry name against the editor function map (dangling either way silently disables a path); (b) cross-check quota/affordability gates — any site using the hosted-only canPayForAiRequest must be guarded by !isCustomEndpointEnabled(), or BYOK users get blocked by a hosted limit. Also: SuggestionLines.js is upstream-identical and must NOT be edited even when it looks fragile; the fork maintains the invariant on its side (sanitizeAiRequestSuggestions always emits an array).

ensureObjectHasProperty only validates the TOP-LEVEL key, so any deeper path on an API response (limits.capabilities.ai.availablePresets) is unverified at runtime despite a non-optional Flow type. Treat nested API-response walks as unchecked and default each level. Also: a bare `npx jest <dir>` in newIDE/app lacks the libGD test artifact, so specs touching global.gd fail — confirm a failure is pre-existing by stashing and re-running before blaming the change.

After finding one unguarded deep API-response walk, sweep the fork-modified files for the same shape rather than fixing one instance: `limits.credits.userBalance.amount` appeared at three more sites after cycle 134's `limits.capabilities.ai.availablePresets`. Extract a single defaulting helper when the same deep read repeats, so the guard cannot drift between copies.

Optional chaining is supported in the app (used in ~8 files) and is the cleanest form for a deep walk on an API response; the fork's Flow files accept it (verified: no new Flow errors, baseline 847 unchanged). The full app Flow baseline is 847 errors and must be compared against stashed HEAD before attributing any error to a change.

The modifiesProject flag is a security-relevant invariant in two places (the read-only run_script filter and the edit-approval prompt), so audit it in BOTH directions: a mutating tool flagged false leaks into read-only scripts, and a read-only tool flagged true is wrongly withheld. Nine of the flags live in EditorFunctions/Extensions/*.js and GameplayTestTools.js, not in EditorFunctions/index.js — a single-file grep reports them as 'absent' and is misleading.

When a bug class is fixed (cycle 129's surrogate-splitting slice), grep for OTHER bare `.slice(0, N)`/`substring` truncations of text that reaches the wire — buildSubAgentReport carried the same defect 9 cycles later. And when adding a helper for a cap, TEST THROUGH THE CALLER: a test that calls truncateReport directly passes even after buildSubAgentReport is reverted to a raw slice; only driving buildSubAgentReport catches it.

The surrogate-splitting truncation appeared THREE times (token budget, sub-agent report, GDD note); each was found only by grepping for the pattern after fixing the previous. When two fork modules both need a tiny pure helper but one already imports the other, add a new leaf module (SafeTruncation.js) rather than importing backwards or duplicating — and record the new file in fork-divergence.json in the same commit, which is what the guard's --update does surgically.

Run fork specs with `npm test` (react-app-rewired with the CRA babel config), NOT a bare `npx jest`: bare jest fails to transform the repo's .ts files (e.g. UseForceUpdate.ts) and reports a SyntaxError that looks like an environmental failure. CORRECTION to cycles 134/138/139: the '3 SpawnSubAgents / libGD-ProjectHelper failures' were NOT environmental — they were a bare-`npx jest` artifact. `npm test -- --testPathPattern=...` (react-app-rewired + CRA babel, with the libGD test artifact already installed) runs the whole AiGeneration directory green: 261/261 across 14 suites, and 449/449 across the 15 AI+AiGeneration suites. Find coverage gaps programmatically: for each fork-modified file, regex its `export const <name>` list and diff against the spec text — that surfaced aiRequestShouldBeWatched / aiRequestHasWorkInProgress / getSubAgentKind, all live in production with no tests. When an unknown enum/id must not crash a turn, pick the fallback by PRIVILEGE, not by convenience: getToolsForRole throwing was load-bearing (it stops a read-only role silently gaining mutations), so the no-throw replacement had to be the read-only subset, not the full toolset. Mutation-check the direction — swapping in the full toolset made the new test show create_scene/run_script being offered. Also: buildSystemPrompt had ZERO coverage despite shaping every prompt; the coverage-gap sweep (regex `export const X` vs the spec text) is what surfaced it.

To test a lock/mutex, the discriminating case is a turn QUEUED WHILE the lock is held (or while the holder throws) — not a later, sequential acquisition, which passes even when the failure path skips release because cleanup still clears the key. Frame the assertion with a timeout race ('queued-ran' vs 'timed-out 500ms') so a deadlock fails the test instead of hanging the suite.

After fixing a bug at one call site of a shared helper (cycle 142's getStudioRole), grep ALL callers: a fifth site in Utils.js had the identical defect and a worse failure mode (it stalled the whole dispatch batch). Also: when a pure helper cannot be unit-tested because its module's import graph pulls in three.js, extract the helper to a leaf module rather than skipping the test — the repo already uses this pattern for SafeTruncation and NonScriptableFunctionNames.

When a function validates one field of a model-authored payload rigorously (generatedEvents here), check its siblings: six nearby fields used `X || []`, which is a truthiness test, not a shape test — `.join`/`for..of` on a truthy non-array throws, and the failure lands in the CONSUMER, far from the cause. Also re-checked this cycle with no change needed: every setTimeout in the fork AI surface uses a fixed literal under 5s (the cycle-125 overflow class needs a user-supplied value), and SIDE_EFFECT_FREE_TOOLS contains no mutating tool (verified against MUTATING_TOOL_NAMES), so the text fallback cannot execute a mutation.

A `X || []` followed by `for..of` is the same trap as `X || []` followed by `.join`: a truthy non-array is not iterable, and it throws in whichever function happens to consume it.
